title: Responsible AI & Data Governance
blurb: Tests where bias comes from, why fairness definitions conflict, how proxy variables let a model discriminate without the protected attribute, SHAP and LIME, robustness testing, the costs of building and running a model, and what GDPR asks of an ML system.

ideas.title: Auditing a model and reading the numbers

questions.prompt: A model is trained to predict "good employees" from a company's past hiring decisions. Those decisions were discriminatory. Which kind of bias does the chapter call this?
options: Label noise. The labels are random errors that cancel out with enough data.
Sample bias. One group has too few rows for the model to learn its pattern.
Historical bias. The training labels record past discrimination, and the model learns it.
Measurement bias. One group's features were recorded with a different, less accurate instrument.
questions.explanation: Historical bias is the case where past decisions were discriminatory, so the training data reflects them directly. Sample bias is about under-representation, and measurement bias is about a group being measured differently. Neither is the point here. The labels are not random noise either. They are systematically skewed, so more data reproduces the skew instead of averaging it away.

refLinks.label: §21.2.1 Bias in ML: Sources and Types

questions.prompt: A team drops the race and gender columns before training. Why can the model still discriminate by race or gender?
options: Other features, like zip code or first name, correlate with them and stand in for them.
The dropped columns stay in the training labels, which the model reads again whenever it makes a prediction.
Dropping a column only hides it from feature importance. The model still trains on it.
Random forests reconstruct dropped columns from the row index unless it is shuffled.
questions.explanation: This is the proxy-variable mechanism. Protected attributes often correlate with innocent-looking features like zip code, name or browsing history, so a model trained without the attribute can still learn it through its proxies. The other options describe mechanisms that don't exist. A dropped column is gone from training, and the model does not see labels at prediction time.

refLinks.label: §21.2.1 Bias in ML: Sources and Types

questions.prompt: In the worked example, the first model uses experience, test score, education, zip code and first name. The demographic group column is in neither model. What does the drop from 0.177 to 0.982 in the Disparate Impact Ratio show?
options: The ratio rose because the second model selects fewer people overall, which shrinks every gap.
The group column leaked into training through the labels, and removing the proxies blocked the leak.
Removing the proxies fixed the disparity. The protected attribute was never there to remove.
Removing any two features from a random forest raises the ratio, because the trees get shallower.
questions.explanation: The demographic column was never a feature, yet the first model discriminated by nearly 5x through zip code and name. Removing those two proxies, with nothing else changed, gave a clean pass. That is the proxy mechanism made visible. The ratio did not rise because fewer people were selected: Group B's rate rose from 0.147 to 0.588. Tree depth is unchanged (max_depth=6 in both).

questions.prompt: A logistics team says zip code predicts delivery time because it tracks commute distance, so it should stay. It also correlates with a protected group. What approach fits the chapter best?
options: Keep it, and add the protected attribute as a feature too, so the model can separate the two effects.
Check this proxy on its own. Measure what it adds in accuracy and what it does to group gaps, then decide.
Remove it. Any feature that correlates with a protected attribute has to go, whatever predictive value it carries.
Keep it. A feature with real predictive value cannot be a proxy, by definition.
questions.explanation: The chapter's trade-offs section says removing proxies can cost accuracy, and fairness audits need domain judgement. That argues for checking each candidate proxy, as Exercise 21.6 asks, rather than a blanket rule. A feature can carry real signal and still act as a proxy, so "it predicts well" doesn't settle it. Adding the protected attribute as a feature does not remove the disparity and creates a new legal problem.

questions.prompt: Which fairness definition asks only that the true-positive rate be equal across groups?
options: Equal opportunity
Equalised odds
Demographic parity
Calibration
questions.explanation: Equal opportunity asks only for equal true-positive rates. It suits cases where missing a qualified person is the main harm. Demographic parity compares positive-prediction rates. Equalised odds asks for equal true-positive and false-positive rates. Calibration asks that a predicted probability means the same thing in every group.

refLinks.label: §21.2.1 Bias in ML: Sources and Types

questions.prompt: A loan-approval system's main harm is turning down applicants who would have repaid. Which fairness definition does the chapter point to?
options: Demographic parity, which equalises approval rates across groups whatever each group's repayment record.
Calibration, which makes a score of 0.7 mean the same repayment chance in every group.
Equalised odds, because it is the only definition that looks at errors at all.
Equal opportunity, which asks that qualified applicants in each group are approved at the same rate.
questions.explanation: When missing a qualified individual is the primary harm, the chapter names equal opportunity. It asks only that qualified people are caught at the same rate in each group. Demographic parity ignores who is qualified. Calibration is about what scores mean, not who gets missed. Equalised odds does look at errors, but it also constrains false positives, which is more than this harm calls for. It is the better fit when both error types cost about the same.

refLinks.label: §21.2.1 Bias in ML: Sources and Types

questions.prompt: A hiring tool satisfies demographic parity exactly. What does that tell you about its false-negative rates by group?
options: They are both zero, because parity is only reachable by a perfect classifier.
Nothing. Equal selection rates can sit alongside very unequal false-negative rates.
They differ by exactly the gap in base rates between the groups.
They are equal, because equal selection rates force equal error rates.
questions.explanation: The chapter gives this exact example: a tool optimised for demographic parity can still have very unequal false-negative rates. Selection rate counts positive predictions. It doesn't say who among the qualified got them. There is no fixed formula linking the two, and parity does not need a perfect classifier.

refLinks.label: §21.2.1 Bias in ML: Sources and Types

questions.prompt: False approvals and false denials both carry real, comparable costs. Which fairness definition fits, and why?
options: Demographic parity, because equal approval rates make the two error types cancel.
Equalised odds, because it equalises both true-positive and false-positive rates across groups.
Calibration, because it is the only definition that refers to both kinds of mistake.
Equal opportunity, because matching true-positive rates also matches false approvals across groups.
questions.explanation: Equalised odds constrains both the true-positive rate (so false-denial rates match) and the false-positive rate (so false-approval rates match). Equal opportunity only looks at the true-positive rate, so it leaves false approvals free to differ. Demographic parity does not look at errors at all. Calibration is about the meaning of scores, not about matching error rates.

refLinks.label: §21.2.1 Bias in ML: Sources and Types

questions.prompt: Which of these are pipeline points the chapter gives for fairness mitigation? Select all that apply.
options: At deployment, hide the model's decisions from the affected people
During training, add a fairness constraint to the loss
After training, set decision thresholds separately per group
Before training, reweight or resample the data, or remove proxy variables
questions.explanation: The chapter lists pre-processing, in-processing and post-processing, in that order. Hiding decisions from the people affected is not mitigation. It would also clash with the GDPR right to explanation covered later in the chapter.

refLinks.label: §21.2.1 Bias in ML: Sources and Types

questions.prompt: In the fairness audit in Listing 21.1, how is the Disparate Impact Ratio computed?
options: The lowest group selection rate divided by the highest
The lowest group accuracy divided by the highest
The gap between group selection rates divided by the overall selection rate
The highest group selection rate divided by the lowest
questions.explanation: The listing computes `rates.min() / rates.max()` over per-group selection rates. That keeps the ratio at or below 1, and the 4/5ths rule wants it at 0.8 or above. Max over min would exceed 1 and flip the test. The ratio uses selection rates, not accuracy.

questions.prompt: An audit finds selection rates of 0.42 for Group A and 0.30 for Group B. What is the Disparate Impact Ratio? Give it to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: The ratio is min over max: 0.30 / 0.42 = 0.714. That is below 0.8, so it fails the 4/5ths rule.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, the proxy-included model selects 0.828 of Group A and 0.147 of Group B. The proxy-free model selects 0.577 and 0.588. By how many percentage points did the absolute gap between the groups shrink? Give one decimal place.
questions.explanation: With proxies the gap is 82.8 − 14.7 = 68.1 points. Without them it is |57.7 − 58.8| = 1.1 points. The gap shrank by 68.1 − 1.1 = 67.0 points. Both groups moved, but the gap collapsed.

questions.prompt: The proxy-included model has a true-positive rate of 0.880 for Group A and 0.183 for Group B. What does that mean for two equally qualified candidates, one from each group?
options: The Group B candidate is about 18% less likely to be hired than an equally qualified Group A candidate.
Group A's candidate is recognised as hireable about 9 times in 10. Group B's, about 1 time in 5.
About 18% of Group B's selected candidates are unqualified, against 88% for Group A.
The model is wrong about 88% of Group A candidates and about 18% of Group B candidates.
questions.explanation: The TPR is the share of truly qualified people the model selects. 0.880 against 0.183 means a qualified Group B candidate is caught about 1 time in 5, against about 9 in 10 for Group A. That is close to a 5x gap, not 18%. The TPR says nothing about how many selected people are unqualified, which would be a precision question, and it is not an error rate.

questions.prompt: A customer says: "We don't collect race or gender, so our model can't be biased." Which reply does the chapter's worked example support?
options: The model could be biased only if the labels were noisy, and the worked example shows noise averages out.
The worked example never used the group column, yet zip code and name carried it. Not collecting an attribute doesn't stop proxies.
That is mostly correct. Proxies only matter for linear models, and the worked example's model was a random forest, so it is safe.
That is correct. Without the protected attribute, no fairness metric can be computed, so there is nothing to fix.
questions.explanation: The worked example is built to rebut this claim. Group was never a feature, and the Disparate Impact Ratio was still 0.177 until the proxies were removed. The model in that example is a random forest, so proxies clearly matter for non-linear models. To audit, you do need group labels, but lacking them hides the bias, it doesn't remove it.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between interpretability and explainability as the chapter uses the terms?
options: An interpretable model can be read directly. Explainability approximates a black box after training.
Interpretability is about global feature importance. Explainability is about why one single prediction came out.
They are two names for the same thing, and the chapter uses them interchangeably.
Explainability means the model is simple. Interpretability means a tool like SHAP was used.
questions.explanation: The callout separates them. Interpretability means the model itself is transparent, like a shallow tree or a linear model's coefficients. Explainability means a technique like SHAP or LIME builds an approximation after the fact. The global versus local split is a different distinction the chapter also draws, and the last option has the two terms backwards.

questions.prompt: Why can TreeExplainer give exact SHAP values quickly, when exact Shapley values are exponential in general?
options: It samples a few feature subsets and scales the result, which is exact for trees.
Trees have at most a handful of features, so checking every subset is cheap.
It uses the tree structure directly, which lets it compute exact values in polynomial time.
It fits a local linear model around each prediction, as LIME does.
questions.explanation: The general computation checks every subset of features, which is exponential. TreeExplainer exploits the tree structure to get exact answers in polynomial time. Sampling gives an approximation, not exact values. Trees can have many features. Fitting a local linear model is how LIME works.

questions.prompt: Procedure 21.2 warns against running KernelExplainer on a full large test set. What is the problem and the fix?
options: It gives wrong signs on large sets, so switch to LIME.
It only works on tree models, so retrain the model as a random forest.
It is slow enough to be impractical, so sample the rows first.
It ignores the baseline on large sets, so pass the expected value explicitly.
questions.explanation: KernelExplainer approximates Shapley values for any model and its cost grows with features times samples. On a big test set that is impractical, so the procedure says always sample. Nothing in the chapter says its signs flip or that it drops the baseline. It is TreeExplainer, not KernelExplainer, that is specific to trees.

questions.prompt: A regulator asks whether a SHAP value shows why a black-box model denied a loan. What answer does the chapter's callout support?
options: Yes, if TreeExplainer was used. Exact values are the same as the model's actual reasoning.
It is a plausible reconstruction by a simpler imitating model, not a record of the model's reasoning.
Yes. SHAP values sum exactly to the prediction, so they show precisely what the model did for that applicant.
No, and interpretable models would not help, because they always cost too much accuracy to use.
questions.explanation: The callout says an explanation is a second model built to imitate the first. It can be faithful without being correct, so it answers "here is a plausible reconstruction". Additivity and exactness are properties of the attribution, not proof of the reasoning. The callout also cites Bell et al. (2022), who found no consistent accuracy penalty for interpretable models in real policy settings.

questions.prompt: What is the LLM counterpart of an adversarial image perturbation?
options: A prompt injection or jailbreak that makes the model ignore its instructions
A request in a language the model saw very little of during its pretraining
A typo in the user's question that lowers answer quality
A long prompt that exceeds the model's context window
questions.explanation: An adversarial image is crafted to flip a prediction while looking normal. The LLM version is text built to make the model ignore its instructions, leak its system prompt, or get past guardrails. The other options are ordinary input problems, not inputs an adversary crafts to break the model.

questions.prompt: Which of these match the chapter's three points for robustness mitigation? Select all that apply.
options: Curating out training data with known attack triggers
Raising the decision threshold until no adversarial example works
Input validation and guardrail layers before the model
Adversarial training on adversarial examples
questions.explanation: The chapter mirrors the fairness structure: before training, curate data; during training, adversarial training; after training, input validation and guardrails. Moving a threshold does not stop a crafted input. The chapter also says no method guarantees robustness.

questions.prompt: What does the chapter give as the realistic goal of robustness work?
options: To earn a one-time robustness certificate the model keeps
To raise the cost of a successful attack, knowing the adversary adapts
To prove the model has no adversarial examples before release
To reach the same accuracy on adversarial inputs as on clean ones
questions.explanation: The chapter says none of the methods guarantees robustness. They raise the cost of an attack. Robustness is a moving target against an adaptive adversary, not a property a model earns once and keeps. That rules out proofs and one-time certificates.

questions.prompt: Why can serving a model end up with a larger carbon footprint than training it?
options: Serving needs the full training data loaded on every request.
Training costs are paid by the cloud provider, so they don't count.
Inference always runs on dirtier grids than training does.
A model trained once may be served billions of times, and the inference cost adds up.
questions.explanation: Training happens once. Inference repeats for every request, so at scale it can outgrow training. That is why the chapter links compression (distillation, quantisation, pruning) to sustainability. Grids depend on region and time, not on the task, and serving does not load the training data.

questions.prompt: Data collected for fraud detection is quietly reused to train a marketing model. Which GDPR principle does that break?
options: Purpose limitation
The right to explanation
The right to erasure
Data minimisation
questions.explanation: Purpose limitation says data collected for one purpose can't silently feed a different model. Data minimisation is about using no more data than necessary. Erasure and explanation are rights a person exercises, and this scenario is about reuse.

questions.prompt: What failure does a data contract prevent?
options: A model breaking quietly after an upstream schema change nobody downstream was told about
A model memorising personal data from training and repeating it word for word in its output
A team training on data it has no legal right to use
A model's carbon cost growing as more users arrive
questions.explanation: A data contract is a formal agreement between producer and consumer on schema, semantics and SLAs. It catches the quiet failure where upstream changes break a model. Memorised PII is handled by redaction, hashing, synthetic data or differential privacy. Legal rights and carbon are separate concerns.

questions.prompt: A team argues that fairness audits, SHAP and red-teaming slow them down, so they will add fairness after launch. Which argument from the chapter's trade-offs section answers them best?
options: Audits can be added later without loss, because fairness metrics only need the final model.
Skipping it costs more: GDPR fines, legal liability, reputational harm. Fairness has to be designed in.
Red-teaming can replace the fairness audit, so they only need to do one of the two.
The work costs nothing, because removing proxy variables never reduces accuracy.
questions.explanation: The chapter concedes the practices cost real time, then argues that skipping them costs more: fines, legal liability and reputational harm. It says "we'll add fairness later" doesn't work as a plan. It does not claim the work is free. It says removing proxies can reduce accuracy. Red-teaming tests robustness, not fairness.

bookExercises.prompt: Explain in your own words why a model can discriminate by demographic group even when the demographic group column itself is never included as a feature.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A demographic group column that's excluded from training can still be discriminated against through proxy variables: other features (zip code, name, browsing history) that happen to correlate strongly with the excluded attribute. The model has no way to "know" it's using a proxy. It just finds whatever pattern in the available features predicts the historically biased label best. If a proxy carries that signal, the model uses it exactly as it would use any other predictive feature.

bookExercises.prompt: Name the fairness metric most appropriate for: (a) a loan-approval system where missing a qualified applicant is the primary harm; (b) a system where both false approvals and false denials carry real, comparable costs.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: (a) Equal Opportunity: missing a qualified applicant (false negative) is explicitly the harm being minimised. (b) Equalised Odds: both false positives and false negatives carrying real cost is exactly equalised odds' target condition (equal TPR *and* FPR across groups).

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 21.4 and Listing 21.5's measured Disparate Impact Ratios (0.177 with proxies, 0.982 without), compute the absolute percentage-point gap in Group A vs. Group B selection rates in both cases, and state which changed more: the gap, or the overall selection rate level.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: With proxies: Group A 0.828 − Group B 0.147 = 0.681 (68.1 percentage points). Without proxies: Group A 0.577 − Group B 0.588 = −0.011 (about 1.1 percentage points, in the opposite direction, and effectively noise). The *gap* changed dramatically, from 68 points to near zero. The *overall selection rate level* also shifted, roughly 48-58% combined, versus the widely split 82.8%/14.7%. But the far more consequential change is the near-total collapse of the gap between groups, not the modest shift in overall level.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 21.1's pattern, explain what a TPR gap of 0.880 vs. 0.183 (this chapter's proxy-included model) means in plain language for a qualified Group B candidate's actual chances, compared to an equally qualified Group A candidate.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A TPR of 0.880 for Group A means 88% of truly qualified Group A candidates are correctly identified as hires. A TPR of 0.183 for Group B means only 18.3% of truly qualified Group B candidates are. In plain terms: an equally qualified Group B candidate has roughly a 1-in-5 chance of being correctly recognised as hireable, versus roughly 9-in-10 for an equally qualified Group A candidate. That's nearly a 5x gap in the odds of a qualified person from each group actually being selected.

bookExercises.prompt: A customer says "we don't collect race or gender, so our model can't be biased." Using this chapter's Worked Example, write the two or three sentences you'd say back.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "Not collecting race or gender directly doesn't prevent discrimination through proxies. This chapter's own measured example shows a model with neither attribute in its feature list still producing a Disparate Impact Ratio of 0.177, entirely through zip code and first name standing in for the excluded attribute. The right check isn't 'did we collect the protected attribute.' It's a fairness audit on the model's actual outputs across whatever demographic groups matter here."

bookExercises.prompt: A team wants to remove all proxy features to guarantee fairness, including features with genuine predictive value like zip code (which might legitimately correlate with commute time for a logistics model). Using this chapter's Trade-offs section, write the case for checking each candidate proxy individually rather than removing all of them by rule.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "A blanket rule removes genuinely useful signal along with the bias. For a logistics model, commute time legitimately correlates with delivery performance regardless of who lives where. Removing zip code entirely could hurt accuracy for no fairness benefit, if it isn't actually acting as a demographic proxy in that context. The better approach is auditing each candidate feature's actual correlation with the sensitive attribute and its actual contribution to any measured disparity, as this chapter's before/after removal comparison did, rather than assuming every feature that *could* be a proxy *is* one in every application."

bookExercises.prompt: Read the Barocas, Hardt, and Narayanan chapter on the impossibility of simultaneously satisfying multiple fairness definitions. Identify the specific condition under which demographic parity and equalised odds become mutually exclusive, and relate it to this chapter's hiring example.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only. Demographic parity and equalised odds become mutually exclusive specifically when the true base rates of the outcome differ between groups, e.g. if Group A and Group B genuinely have different underlying qualification rates in the population. Satisfying equal selection rates (demographic parity) while the true positive rate must also be equal (equalised odds) is only simultaneously achievable when the groups' true positive rates in the data already match. That's rarely the case when historical bias has shaped the labels themselves, as in this chapter's hiring example, where Group B's true hire rate was deliberately lowered by construction.
